Final open syllable, short a as in 'ah.'

pronunciation.approximation: 'GOO-lah' — the name is the Akkadian feminine of 'great,' an epithet worn as a name.

pronunciation.note: Gula is single-tier Tier 2: the ASCII form loses nothing distinctive, since the Akkadian name contains no sound a diacritic would preserve in this restoration. The name itself is an epithet — 'The Great One' — and the doublet Ninisina shows the tradition naming her by her city before it named her by her size.

domains.title: Gula
domains.subtitle: Healing
domains.lead: Gula is the great healing goddess of Mesopotamia — 'The Great One,' Lady of Isin, wife of Ninurta, and divine patroness of medicine. Doctors, exorcists, and suffering patients alike called on her to look kindly on the sick; her dogs stood guard at the gates of her temples for over a thousand years.

cards.name: Divine Physician
cards.desc: She is called 'the great doctress' in hymns; medical incantations open by invoking her gaze on the patient.

cards.name: Lady of Isin
cards.desc: Her city and temple, Isin's E-gal-maḥ, made her name a byword for healing across the Near East.

cards.name: Consort of Ninurta
cards.desc: Wife of the warrior-god, she softens his storms — healing joined to kingship and order.

cards.name: Mistress of the Dogs
cards.desc: Her sacred dogs guarded temple gates and received votive burials; they carried prayers upward.

symbols.name: The Dog
symbols.meaning: Her sacred animal; clay dog figurines were dedicated and buried at the gates of her temples at Isin and Nippur

symbols.name: The Healing Hand
symbols.meaning: Her touch that 'restores to life' — the gesture invoked at the head of medical incantations

symbols.name: The Binding Bandage
symbols.meaning: She who 'binds up' wounds; the idiom survives in Akkadian medical phrases for closing an injury

symbols.name: The Medicinal Herb
symbols.meaning: The drug of life' (šammu ša balāṭi) that she bestows, named beside her in therapeutic texts

symbols.name: E-gal-maḥ
symbols.meaning: Her 'Exalted Great House' at Isin, where the sick slept for dream diagnoses

mythology.lead: Gula's mythology is mostly hymn, not narrative — the Mesopotamian tradition honored her in praise poetry and medical incantation rather than epic. What the texts build is a portrait: the goddess who looks at the sick and restores them, the queen of Isin whose greatness outranks the other gods.

myths.title: Bulluṭsa-rabi Sings Her Praise
myths.text: The most famous poem to Gula is the long hymn of the devotee Bulluṭsa-rabi ('O Great Lady, soothe my heart'), known from dozens of Old Babylonian and later copies. Line by line it outranks her against the other great goddesses — her power exceeds theirs, her command governs life and death, and even the gods themselves are her patients. The hymn names her city, Isin, and calls her 'the great healer who revives the dead' — hyperbole that maps her onto no single myth but onto every sickbed. The poem survives in Foster's Before the Muses and the Pennsylvania Sumerian/Assyriological corpora. The poet's very name — Bulluṭsa-rabi, 'O Great Lady, soothe my heart' — casts him as a courtier, and the flattery is systematic: each rival goddess is praised at length precisely so that Gula can surpass her. It tells us what a myth could not:It tells us what a myth could not: that healing itself was worshiped, and that the doctor's hope had a goddess to address.

myths.title: The Prayer of the Sufferer
myths.text: Babylonian penitential psalms give Gula the words of the desperate. One such prayer, 'I kneel before you, daughter of Anu... my affliction is grievous, my wound severe' (Foster, Before the Muses), has the patient catalog his sins before the goddess, begging her to 'look upon me and let your heart be soothed.' In Ludlul bēl nēmeqi ('I Will Praise the Lord of Wisdom'), the righteous sufferer's restoration comes through the diviner and exorcist whose rites Gula empowers. The theology is striking for its psychology: illness is no pure accident but a rupture — with the gods, with one's city, with one's own past — so the cure must begin in confession before it can proceed to the drug. No story here — and that is the point:No story here — and that is the point: the tradition put its theology of illness into first-person speech, making every sufferer briefly the hero of his own rescue.

myths.title: From Bau to Gula
myths.text: Before she was Gula of Isin, the healing goddess was Bau of Lagash, daughter of An and wife of Ningirsu, celebrated in the inscriptions of Gudea (c. 2125 BCE) and in Sumerian hymns as the compassionate one who hears prayer. As Isin rose under the dynasties of the early second millennium, her local goddess Ninisina absorbed Bau's character and acquired the Akkadian epithet Gula, 'The Great One'; her consort became the storm-warrior Ninurta (Jacobsen, The Treasures of Darkness, 1976). Her names multiplied as her cities changed hands: Ninkarrak guarded the northern caravan towns, while other districts knew her as Nintinugga — a theonymic heap that is the fossil record of Mesopotamian geopolitics. The merger showsThe merger shows how goddesses traveled in Mesopotamia — not by conquest but by translation, one city's Lady becoming every city's healer.

myths.title: Votive Guardians of Isin
myths.text: Excavations at Isin — modern Išān Baḥriyāt, dug by the Bavarian Academy under Barthel Hrouda from 1973 — uncovered Gula's temple precinct and, in it, terracotta dogs: seated, collar-wearing, many bearing the inscriptions of donors ('to Gula, for the life of...'). Buried at the temple gate, they guarded the threshold where the sick crossed into the goddess's care. Similar dog burials marked her shrines at Nippur and Adab. Some of the buried dogs carry inked labels — 'to Gula, for the life of So-and-so, his owner' — letting us watch named individuals kneeling at the temple gate, and the figures themselves are no lapdogs but the fleet pariah dogs of the Near Eastern street. The sources give no myth explaining the dog;The sources give no myth explaining the dog; the archaeology supplies one silently: at the boundary between sickness and healing stands a faithful animal, patient as hope itself.

lore.syncretism: Gula is a syncretism achieved across two thousand years. She began as Ninisina of Isin, absorbed Bau of Lagash, took the Akkadian title 'Gula,' and acquired a northern double in Ninkarrak of Sippar — the CAD treats the names as largely interchangeable in late texts. As Isin's political star set under the rising Babylonian and Assyrian empires, her goddess traveled: dog figurines dedicated to Gula appear at Nippur, Adab, and in Assyrian collections, and her incantations were copied from one medical library to another across the whole cuneiform world. In the first millennium her iconography stabilized — the goddess with her dog — and it is in this form that Hellenistic scholars compared her to Hygieia, the Greek goddess of health. Modern Mesopotamian studies treat her as the paradigmatic case of how a local healing deity became the divine patron of an entire medical tradition.
lore.culturalLegacy: Gula's cult was centered on Isin, where her temple drew the sick from across southern Mesopotamia; her priests were the physicians and exorcists whose dual therapy — drug and incantation — defined Mesopotamian medicine. Her legacy outlived her temples. The medical manuscripts that invoke her, copied and recopied into the Seleucid period, became the foundation documents of Assyriology's study of ancient medicine, and her clay dogs are today among the most reproduced Mesopotamian objects in world museums (Berlin's Vorderasiatisches Museum holds celebrated examples). Her name persists quietly in the modern world as a byword for veterinary and medical care, and in scholarly usage 'Gula' has become shorthand for the entire theology of healing in the ancient Near East — a reputation two millennia of doctors would have recognized.
lore.extendedMeditation: Gula embodies a proposition most ancient theologies only imply: that healing is a form of greatness. Her very name is the Akkadian word for 'great' in the feminine — as if the culture had looked for the largest possible title and given it to the one who closes wounds. The Babylonian doctor, standing between the drug list and the incantation, addressed her before both, acknowledging that technique without mercy is not medicine. There is something striking in a warrior civilization's supreme goddess of care being the wife of its storm-god: the spear and the bandage married. To read her hymns is to watch a civilization think through suffering — not explaining it away, as Job's comforters tried, but giving it a face that looks back, 'soothes the heart,' and sometimes says yes. That is a theology a sickbed can actually use.
lore.archaeology: The core evidence is the temple precinct at Isin (Išān Baḥriyāt), excavated by the Bavarian Academy's team from 1973 onward: Gula's E-gal-maḥ, rebuilt across centuries, yielded foundation inscriptions, votive deposits, and her famous terracotta dogs — some inscribed with donors' prayers. Her shrines at Nippur (excavated by the University of Chicago and University of Pennsylvania expeditions) produced further dog burials and medical tablets, tying her cult directly to the practice of medicine; a Gula temple is also attested at Adab. Textual archaeology is equally rich: the Old Babylonian hymn of Bulluṭsa-rabi survives in scores of copies from Nippur, Ur, and Assyrian libraries, making Gula's praise one of the most widely duplicated religious poems in cuneiform.
